title: Master Compiled Vertices and Historical Locations
description: Unified compilation of all geospatial vertices, locations, and building footprints across Ireland, Great Britain, Canada, the Middle East, China, India, Japan, and Algeria.

vertices.name: Weavers' Hall, the Coombe
vertices.perspective: Dublin Guild of Weavers / Free trade tariff equalization
vertices.footprint_notes: Guild hall of 1745 at 14 Lower Coombe. Financed in part by David Digges La Touche with a statue of George II; demolished in 1965 for road realignment and social housing. No mapped historic footprint in OSM.

vertices.name: Stove Tenter House
vertices.perspective: Thomas Pleasants / Industrial relief for Liberties weavers
vertices.footprint_notes: Extant building footprint on Brickfield Lane between Cork Street and Brown Street South; constructed 1815 by philanthropist Thomas Pleasants to allow weavers to dry cloth in heated rooms.

vertices.name: Manchester
vertices.perspective: the mill owner / mechanized competition
vertices.footprint_notes: City centroid representing the industrial textile mill owners who benefited from the tariff removal under Article VI of the Act of Union.

vertices.name: Devon Commission hearing venue (Kilrush)
vertices.perspective: Rev. Malachi Duggan's testimony on Crotty's eviction
vertices.footprint_notes: Kilrush courthouse sitting of the Devon Commission on August 23, 1844, where Rev. Malachi Duggan testified (witness no. 608) on tenure-at-will and the 1832 eviction of Crotty.

vertices.name: Royal Dublin Society Botanic Gardens (National Botanic Gardens)
vertices.perspective: David Moore / Royal Dublin Society blight discovery
vertices.footprint_notes: Closed way polygon covering the 19.5-hectare National Botanic Gardens precinct along the River Tolka where curator David Moore identified Phytophthora infestans on August 20, 1845.

vertices.name: HM Treasury / Downing Street
vertices.perspective: Peel's government / cabinet crisis and Corn Law repeal
vertices.footprint_notes: Prime Minister Sir Robert Peel's official residence and executive cabinet room on Downing Street during the 1845-1846 crisis.

vertices.name: HM Treasury (Government Offices Great George Street / GOGGS)
vertices.perspective: Charles Trevelyan / Treasury relief administration
vertices.footprint_notes: Government Offices Great George Street (GOGGS), main building of HM Treasury on Horse Guards Road and Great George Street.

vertices.name: Mount Trenchard
vertices.perspective: Thomas Spring-Rice, Lord Monteagle (letter recipient)
vertices.footprint_notes: Estate of Lord Monteagle in County Limerick, to whom Charles Trevelyan addressed his October 9, 1846 letter outlining providential non-intervention policy.

vertices.name: South Reen, parish of Myross
vertices.perspective: Nicholas Cummins / eye-witness investigation of Skibbereen famine
vertices.footprint_notes: Townland on the eastern side of Castlehaven Harbour visited on December 15, 1846 by Cork magistrate Nicholas Cummins, published in The Times on December 24, 1846.

vertices.name: Curragh Chase House
vertices.perspective: Stephen de Vere's ancestral seat and estate
vertices.footprint_notes: Building footprint of Curraghchase House (18th-century country house ruin) inside Curraghchase Forest Park; ancestral home of Sir Stephen de Vere.

vertices.name: Grosse Île quarantine station
vertices.place: Gulf of Saint Lawrence, Quebec, Canada
vertices.perspective: emigrant destination / quarantine station and cemetery
vertices.footprint_status: mapped as point only (island place; station not mapped)
vertices.footprint_notes: Island in Saint-Antoine-de-l'Isle-aux-Grues, Montmagny. Site of the 1847 typhus epidemic and 5,424 burials. Mapped as an island node; specific hospital buildings lack OSM polygons.

vertices.name: 14 Henrietta Street (Encumbered Estates Court)
vertices.perspective: Encumbered Estates Court / Allan Pollok purchases
vertices.footprint_notes: Georgian townhouse at 14 Henrietta Street; the Encumbered Estates Commission sat here from 1849, holding auctions in converted rear stables.

vertices.name: Lismanny House
vertices.place: near Ballinasloe, East Galway / Creggs, Roscommon, Ireland
vertices.perspective: Allan Pollok's consolidated estate residence
vertices.footprint_notes: Mansion built by Scottish improver Allan Pollok after purchasing 25,234 acres across East Galway and Creggs through the Encumbered Estates Court. Not mapped in OSM.

vertices.name: Cathedral of the Assumption (Synod of Thurles venue)
vertices.perspective: Archbishop Paul Cullen / National Synod of Thurles (1850)
vertices.footprint_notes: Cathedral of the Assumption, Thurles; site of the first national synod held in Ireland since 1642, opening August 22, 1850 under Archbishop Paul Cullen.

vertices.name: Archbishop's House
vertices.perspective: Cardinal Paul Cullen's Dublin archiepiscopal see
vertices.footprint_notes: Archbishop's House in Drumcondra, official residence of the Archbishop of Dublin.

vertices.name: Lough Mask House
vertices.place: near The Neale, County Mayo, Ireland
vertices.perspective: Captain Charles Boycott / tenant isolation campaign
vertices.footprint_notes: Residence of Captain Charles Cunningham Boycott, land agent to the Earl of Erne. Site of the original 1880 'boycott' campaign. Not delineated in OSM.

vertices.name: Ballinrobe
vertices.perspective: the local merchant boycott
vertices.footprint_notes: Town near Lough Mask where local shopkeepers refused service to Charles Boycott and Land League leader Fr. John O'Malley posted placards.

vertices.name: Claremorris railway station
vertices.perspective: arrival and departure of the Orange relief expedition
vertices.footprint_notes: Railway station where fifty volunteers from Cavan and Monaghan arrived under military escort in November 1880 to harvest Boycott's crops.

vertices.name: Hayes's Commercial Hotel
vertices.place: Liberty Square, Thurles, County Tipperary, Ireland
vertices.perspective: Founding of the Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA) / 1887 IRB takeover
vertices.footprint_notes: Hotel on Liberty Square in Thurles; the billiard room served as the founding locus of the GAA on November 1, 1884, and the site of the November 1887 convention.

vertices.name: Gaelic League founding site
vertices.perspective: Douglas Hyde / non-political cultural revival
vertices.footprint_notes: Founded on July 31, 1893 in central Dublin by Douglas Hyde, Eoin MacNeill, and others to revive the Irish language outside of party politics.

vertices.name: Dundalk ard-fheis venue
vertices.perspective: IRB takeover motion and resignation of Douglas Hyde (1915)
vertices.footprint_notes: Venue of the July 29, 1915 Gaelic League ard-fheis in Dundalk, where IRB delegates passed a motion adopting a free Ireland as an explicit aim, prompting Hyde's resignation.

vertices.name: Carton House
vertices.perspective: Duke of Leinster estate trustees / Wyndham Land Act 1903
vertices.footprint_notes: Primary country palace building footprint within Carton Demesne; ancestral seat of the Dukes of Leinster sold in September 1903 under the Wyndham Act.

vertices.name: Athy
vertices.perspective: Matthew Minch and the large-tenant negotiating committee
vertices.footprint_notes: Town where affluent tenant farmers met on September 15, 1903, choosing eighteen delegates to settle purchase terms for the entire Leinster estate.

vertices.name: Castledermot
vertices.perspective: John Keogh and the excluded smallholders
vertices.footprint_notes: Meeting site on September 27, 1903 of marginal southern tenants forced to accept the Athy terms despite protests against 'the big bugs about Athy'.

vertices.name: The Curragh Camp
vertices.perspective: Brigadier General Hubert Gough and the Curragh Mutiny (March 1914)
vertices.footprint_notes: Main British Army military camp in Ireland where approximately sixty officers threatened resignation rather than enforce Home Rule against Ulster.

vertices.name: Larne Harbour
vertices.place: County Antrim, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom
vertices.perspective: Major Frederick Crawford / UVF gun-running (Mountjoy II)
vertices.footprint_notes: Harbour where 25,000 German rifles and ammunition were landed for the Ulster Volunteer Force on April 24-25, 1914 without state interference.

vertices.name: Howth Harbour
vertices.perspective: Erskine Childers, Molly Childers, and the Asgard gun-running
vertices.footprint_notes: Harbour where the yacht Asgard landed 900 German Mauser rifles for the Irish Volunteers on July 26, 1914.

vertices.name: Bachelors Walk
vertices.perspective: King's Own Scottish Borderers firing on unarmed civilians
vertices.footprint_notes: Dublin quay where King's Own Scottish Borderers fired on and bayoneted civilians on July 26, 1914, killing four and wounding over thirty.

vertices.name: British Residency (Cairo)
vertices.perspective: Sir Henry McMahon / McMahon-Hussein correspondence
vertices.footprint_notes: Headquarters of His Majesty's High Commissioner at Cairo, from which the October 24, 1915 letter containing the ambiguous Syrian exclusion clause was dispatched.

vertices.name: Mecca
vertices.perspective: Sharif Hussein bin Ali / leadership of the Arab Revolt
vertices.footprint_notes: Seat of Sharif Hussein bin Ali, who launched the Arab Revolt in June 1916 based on his interpretation of McMahon's letters.

vertices.name: British Foreign Office
vertices.perspective: Sykes-Picot Agreement / Arthur Balfour's declaration
vertices.footprint_notes: Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, King Charles Street; site of diplomatic negotiations for Sykes-Picot (1916) and drafting of the Balfour Declaration (1917).

vertices.name: Amman
vertices.perspective: Sharif Hussein's exile and death (1931)
vertices.footprint_notes: Capital of Transjordan under King Abdullah I, where Sharif Hussein died on June 4, 1931 following his abdication and exile to Cyprus.

vertices.name: Cathal Brugha Barracks (Portobello Barracks)
vertices.perspective: Francis Sheehy-Skeffington execution / Bowen-Colthurst
vertices.footprint_notes: Military barracks in Rathmines where Captain John Bowen-Colthurst executed Francis Sheehy-Skeffington, Thomas Dickson, and Patrick McIntyre without court-martial on April 26, 1916.

vertices.name: General Post Office (GPO)
vertices.perspective: Headquarters of the 1916 Provisional Government
vertices.footprint_notes: Main headquarters of the 1916 Easter Rising rebels, where the Proclamation of the Irish Republic was read by Patrick Pearse.

vertices.name: Kilmainham Gaol (Stonebreakers' Yard)
vertices.perspective: Execution site of 1916 Rising rebel leaders
vertices.footprint_notes: Historic gaol compound where fifteen rebel leaders, including Pearse, Clarke, and Connolly, were executed by British firing squad between May 3 and 12, 1916.

vertices.name: Pearse Street Garda Station (former DMP G Division HQ)
vertices.place: Pearse Street (Great Brunswick Street), Dublin, Ireland
vertices.perspective: Michael Collins and Ned Broy / G Division files infiltration
vertices.footprint_notes: Historic Dublin Metropolitan Police detective division headquarters entered on the night of April 7, 1919 by Michael Collins and Seán Nunan via Detective Sergeant Ned Broy.

vertices.name: Mansion House (Round Room)
vertices.perspective: Inaugural meeting of Dáil Éireann (January 21, 1919)
vertices.footprint_notes: Official mayoral residence on Dawson Street; the Round Room (way/275474137) hosted the First Dáil when it declared the Irish Republic on January 21, 1919.

vertices.name: Soloheadbeg Ambush Site
vertices.perspective: 3rd Tipperary Brigade IRA / opening ambush of War of Independence
vertices.footprint_notes: Roadside monument node in Soloheadbeg townland marking the January 21, 1919 shooting of RIC constables McDonnell and O'Connell by Dan Breen, Seán Treacy, and comrades.

vertices.name: Balbriggan
vertices.perspective: Sack of Balbriggan by Black and Tans (September 1920)
vertices.footprint_notes: Coastal town where Black and Tans burned Deeds, Templar & Co's factory and dozens of houses on September 20, 1920, killing civilians Lawless and Gibbons.

vertices.name: Patrick Street / City Hall (Cork)
vertices.perspective: Burning of Cork by Auxiliaries and British forces (December 1920)
vertices.footprint_notes: Commercial center and City Hall of Cork, burned on December 11, 1920 in reprisal for the Dillon's Cross ambush; fire brigade hoses were cut during the blaze.

vertices.name: Croke Park
vertices.perspective: Bloody Sunday massacre (November 21, 1920)
vertices.footprint_notes: National Gaelic athletic stadium footprint; site where mixed British forces opened fire into a crowd of 10,000 spectators during a Dublin vs. Tipperary match, killing fourteen.

vertices.name: 10 Downing Street
vertices.perspective: Signing of the Anglo-Irish Treaty (December 6, 1921)
vertices.footprint_notes: Official residence of the British Prime Minister where Lloyd George issued his 'immediate and terrible war' ultimatum and the Treaty was signed at 2:20 AM.

vertices.name: National Concert Hall (Earlsfort Terrace)
vertices.perspective: Dáil Éireann Anglo-Irish Treaty debates (Dec 1921 - Jan 1922)
vertices.footprint_notes: Former University College Dublin / Royal University building on Earlsfort Terrace where Dáil Éireann debated and ratified the Treaty by 64 votes to 57 on January 7, 1922.

vertices.name: Béal na mBláth Ambush Site
vertices.place: Béal na mBláth, County Cork, Ireland
vertices.perspective: Assassination of Michael Collins (August 22, 1922)
vertices.footprint_notes: Roadside memorial monument on the R585 road marking the spot where Provisional Government Chairman Michael Collins was ambushed and killed during the Civil War.

vertices.name: Colonial Office building
vertices.perspective: Winston Churchill's recruitment instruction to Tudor (Spring 1922)
vertices.footprint_status: not found as a distinct mapped footprint
vertices.footprint_notes: Victorian Colonial Office building on Whitehall / Downing Street. Rebranded and integrated into modern Whitehall offices; no separate historic polygon exists.

vertices.name: Haifa Port
vertices.perspective: Landing of the British Section of the Palestine Gendarmerie (April 30, 1922)
vertices.footprint_notes: Docks where 760 recruits under Tudor, primarily former Black and Tans and Auxiliaries, arrived to establish the Palestine Gendarmerie.

vertices.name: Western Wall
vertices.perspective: Douglas Duff / Yom Kippur partition screen removal (September 23, 1928)
vertices.footprint_notes: Western retaining wall of the Temple Mount compound; flashpoint where Douglas Duff and police removed a screen on Yom Kippur 1928, precipitating the 1929 riots.

vertices.name: Jerusalem Police Command
vertices.perspective: Douglas Duff's police jurisdiction / Mandate urban policing
vertices.footprint_notes: Urban center of Mandatory Jerusalem, headquarters of the Palestine Police District Command where former Black and Tan methods were applied.

vertices.name: Ya'bad Cave / Battle Site
vertices.place: near Jenin, Mandatory Palestine / West Bank
vertices.perspective: Death of Sheikh Izz ad-Din al-Qassam (November 20, 1935)
vertices.footprint_notes: Forested cave near Ya'bad where Sheikh Izz ad-Din al-Qassam made his final stand against British police, sparking the 1936-1939 Arab Revolt.

vertices.name: Istiqlal Mosque
vertices.perspective: Izz ad-Din al-Qassam's pulpit and organizational headquarters
vertices.footprint_notes: Building footprint of Istiqlal Mosque in Haifa's Wadi Salib; pulpit where al-Qassam preached social justice and anti-colonial resistance.

vertices.name: King David Hotel
vertices.perspective: Irgun bombing of British Civil Secretariat and Military HQ (July 22, 1946)
vertices.footprint_notes: Hotel building footprint on King David Street; southwest wing housing the Mandate secretariat was destroyed with milk-churn explosives, killing 91 people.

vertices.name: Houses of Parliament / Palace of Westminster
vertices.perspective: February 1947 UN referral announcement and withdrawal declaration
vertices.footprint_notes: Palace of Westminster multipolygon encompassing the House of Commons and House of Lords, where the decision to terminate the Palestine Mandate was announced.

vertices.name: Patna Opium Factory (Gulzarbagh)
vertices.perspective: British East India Company opium monopoly and processing
vertices.footprint_notes: EIC opium agency and manufacture center along the Ganges where poppy from Bihar was inspected, processed into cakes, and packed for auction.

vertices.name: Ghazipur Opium Factory (Government Opium and Alkaloid Works)
vertices.perspective: British East India Company cultivation and production agency
vertices.footprint_notes: Established 1820 on the Ganga riverside; remains one of the largest legal alkaloid factories. Mapped as an industrial polygon.

vertices.name: The Exchange Rooms (Calcutta Auction Houses)
vertices.place: Dalhousie Square (Tank Square), Calcutta / Kolkata, India
vertices.perspective: EIC opium auctions to private country merchants
vertices.footprint_notes: Financial auction rooms in Dalhousie Square where the Company sold chests to private traders (Jardine Matheson, Sassoons, etc.) to shift legal smuggling risk.

vertices.name: Lintin Island (Neilingding Island)
vertices.perspective: British offshore receiving hulks and smuggling base
vertices.footprint_notes: Offshore anchorage in the Pearl River Delta where foreign clippers transferred opium to permanently moored receiving ships and armed Chinese 'fast crabs'.

vertices.name: Humen Strait (Boca Tigris) / Humen Pearl River Bridge
vertices.place: Pearl River Delta, Dongguan, Guangdong, China
vertices.perspective: Qing coastal fortifications and Lin Zexu's opium destruction (1839)
vertices.footprint_notes: Strategic river narrows leading to Guangzhou, guarded by the Bogue forts. Site of Commissioner Lin Zexu's destruction of 20,000 chests of opium at Humen in June 1839.

vertices.name: Xiguan (Thirteen Factories Area / Liwan District)
vertices.perspective: Hong merchants, foreign trade factories, and smoke dens
vertices.footprint_notes: Commercial district west of old Guangzhou's walls containing the Thirteen Factories foreign enclave and subsequent urban opium-smoking establishments.

vertices.name: Weishan Poppy Fields
vertices.perspective: domestic Chinese opium cultivation in Yunnan borderlands
vertices.footprint_notes: Highland interior region of southwestern China where domestic poppy cultivation expanded in the 1820s-1830s to replace imported coastal opium.

vertices.name: El-Fuleh (Modern Afula)
vertices.perspective: Arab fellahin tenant village evicted in 1925 / American Zion Commonwealth
vertices.footprint_notes: Original Arab agricultural tenant village purchased by the American Zion Commonwealth from the Sursock family in 1925, resulting in fellahin displacement.

vertices.name: Jezreel Valley (Marj ibn Amir)
vertices.perspective: Ottoman Land Code 1858 / Sursock purchases and land consolidation
vertices.footprint_notes: Broad fertile plain in northern Israel sold by the Ottoman Porte in 1872 to the Beirut-based Sursock banking family and later acquired for Zionist settlement.

vertices.name: Tel Maresha (Marisa)
vertices.place: Bet Guvrin-Maresha, Shephelah / Judean Foothills, Israel
vertices.perspective: Hasmonean conquest of Idumea / John Hyrcanus conversion policy (c. 110 BCE)
vertices.footprint_notes: Archaeological tell and subterranean complex in the Shephelah; major Hellenistic Idumean center conquered by Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus around 110 BCE.

vertices.name: Tulkarm
vertices.perspective: Hannun and Hajj Ibrahim families / 1858 Land Code municipal consolidation
vertices.footprint_notes: Subdistrict seat where multazim tax-farmers consolidated title over surrounding communal musha lands under the Tapu Law of December 14, 1858.

vertices.name: Saffarin
vertices.place: Bani Sa'b, Tulkarm Governorate, West Bank, Palestine
vertices.perspective: Dar Hasan hamula / Hannun family ancestral village
vertices.footprint_notes: Village southeast of Tulkarm, ancestral seat of the Huwaytat-descended Hannun lineage before their migration to Tulkarm town.

vertices.name: Kur
vertices.place: Bani Sa'b, Tulkarm Governorate, West Bank, Palestine
vertices.perspective: Jayyusi clan / hereditary throne village
vertices.footprint_notes: Historic throne village of the Jayyusi sheikhs commanding the Bani Sa'b subdistrict prior to the centralization of the 1858 Land Code.

vertices.name: Qasr al-Barqawi
vertices.place: Shufa, Tulkarm Governorate, West Bank, Palestine
vertices.perspective: Isa al-Barqawi / throne fortress and regional tax-farming
vertices.footprint_notes: Restored Ottoman fortified manor of the Barqawi clan in Shufa, commanding regional agrarian dues and levies.

vertices.name: Qaqun Fortress
vertices.place: Tulkarm Subdistrict / Sharon Plain, Central District, Israel
vertices.perspective: Mamluk tower / Ottoman nahiya administrative center
vertices.footprint_notes: Archaeological mound and Mamluk tower marking the historic administrative center of the Qaqun subdistrict.

vertices.name: Sublime Porte (Bab-ı Ali)
vertices.perspective: Tanzimat Council / drafting of the 1858 Ottoman Land Code
vertices.footprint_notes: Central government complex of the Ottoman Empire where Mustafa Reşid Pasha, Âli Pasha, and Ahmet Cevdet Pasha drafted the Land Code under European debt pressure.

vertices.name: Tokyo (Meiji Government)
vertices.perspective: 1873 Chiso Kaisei (Land Tax Reform) / defensive modernization
vertices.footprint_notes: Imperial capital where the Meiji government abolished feudal domain tenure and instituted private certificates and cash land tax to fund defensive state modernization.

vertices.name: Algiers (French Colonial Administration)
vertices.perspective: Auguste Warnier / Warnier Law of 1873 and forced licitation
vertices.footprint_notes: Seat of the French Governor-General of Algeria where the Warnier Law applied French Civil Code Article 815 to force partition and auction of collective indigenous melk land.

vertices.name: Qasim al-Ahmad
vertices.perspective: Sheikh of Jamma'in subdistrict; primary leader of the 1834 uprising

vertices.name: 'Abdullah al-Jarrar
vertices.perspective: Regional leader and commander based out of the fortified stronghold of Sanur

vertices.name: 'Isa al-Barqawi
vertices.perspective: Sheikh of Shufa and co-leader of the northern regional rebel forces

vertices.name: 'Isa al-Amr
vertices.perspective: Leader of the highland clans and commander of the Hebron rebel forces

vertices.name: 'Abd al-Jabir Barghouti
vertices.perspective: Clan leader who mobilized the village militias across the Bani Zeid region

vertices.name: Mas'ud al-Madi
vertices.perspective: Governor and leader of the coastal rebellion around Acre and Mount Carmel

vertices.name: Aqil Agha
vertices.perspective: Hawwara irregular commander leading forces across the Galilee

vertices.name: Duwaikhi al-Samir
vertices.perspective: Bedouin chief who initially sheltered Qasim al-Ahmad during the Egyptian pursuit

vertices.name: Jabr Abu Ghush
vertices.perspective: Head of the Abu Ghosh clan controlling the western approaches to Jerusalem

vertices.name: Muhammad Damoor
vertices.perspective: Local preacher who incited the 33-day attack on the Jewish quarter of Safed
